agent_explanations_oldest_first.text: This split is informative. On problems the original already answered in plain mode, the edit changed nothing: accuracy 24.0% → 24.0%, cut 32.9% → 34.2%. So amplifying the direction causes no measurable collateral damage. On problems that switched from markdown to plain, accuracy rose from 13.6% to 17.3%, but their cut rate nearly doubled, from 22.7% to 40%. The mode switch helps reasoning, and plain mode's loop-proneness eats most of the gain. So loops are the bottleneck in both lines of work, and a combined edit (mode switch plus loop repair) is the most promising path. To understand how loops start, I'll locate in each original looping answer from pass 2 the first line that duplicates an earlier line. Then I'll check the logprob of its first token, the moment the model commits to repeating. If that decision is often a close call (probability well below 1) and the duplicated lines are short "The X is Y." restatements, the onset is a soft decision that a targeted push could change. If repetition is already near-certain at onset, the attractor forms earlier.

Most loops start with a soft decision in plain-mode text. The first token of the first duplicated line often has a logprob of -0.2 to -0.9 (e.g. "The number of plates that were added is 37.", "The length of the board ... is 111 cm."). Once a duplicate has begun, though, copying is near-certain (-0.013 per token). The repeated lines are restatements of an already computed fact, so the model stops making progress and copies its own recent line. The near-deterministic copying is likely carried by attention heads that look up the previous occurrence and copy the next token (induction-style). MLP neurons didn't matter, so I'll look at attention directly. I'll request attention patterns at the four full-attention layers (5, 11, 17, 23) for two plain-mode looping texts. For every head I'll then measure, on copied tokens, the attention mass on the "induction target": the position just after the earlier occurrence of the current token's context. One or two heads putting a large share of attention there, far more than on novel tokens, would identify loop-copying heads to test with graded ablation.

These are two plain-mode looping texts of 897 and 879 tokens, under the 2,048 limit. I'll request attention patterns at the four full-attention layers on the original model, along with token logprobs.

The attention patterns arrived: 4 heads × 896 × 896 at each of the four full-attention layers. A note on indexing: these sequence lengths (896, 878) are one token shorter than my tokenizer count, because tok.encode adds a BOS on top of the literal "<bos>". So my prompt lengths are overcounted by one. That only shifts group boundaries by one token and doesn't affect the copy labels, which come from the returned input_ids. Now the head analysis. For each query position q whose next token is a copy (the 8-gram ending at q occurred earlier, at position p), I'll measure each head's attention to p+1 (induction target: the token that came next last time) and to p (same-token match). I'll compare with the attention given to the same relative positions for novel queries. A head with large induction mass on copied queries would be a loop-copying head.
